absent: Exact numeric values and bit positions for control MSRs, capability and bug identifiers, and prctl result codes.
Implementations of per-task predicate and mutator helpers for store bypass, indirect branch, and thread-flag access plus the flag publisher.
Semantics of prediction barrier, control MSR writer, strict and conditional branch updaters, idle-clear branches, and SMT helpers.
Full update phase of early mitigation selection beyond the truncated fragment and the remaining mitigation selectors.
Locking and concurrency rules for per-task prctl setters and getters and for mitigation selection variables.
Return-thunk targets, prediction-command values, page-table and memory-map helpers, and hypervisor flush states.
Stability guarantees of logging prefixes and diagnostic message strings beyond diagnostics.

findings.text: Task-level speculation controls are exposed through set and get dispatchers that route three distinct vulnerability selectors to dedicated handlers and reject unknown selectors with a device error.

Store bypass task policy is governed by a global mode gate plus persistent per-task attributes for disabled, forced, and no-exec states. Only two global modes permit user changes; forced state is sticky and forbids re-enabling, while no-exec records a one-way exec-related restriction. Queries combine global mode and task attributes into enable, disable, force-disable, no-exec, or unaffected indications.

Indirect branch task policy distinguishes globally unrestricted operation, user-controllable operation, and enforced-restriction operation. In unrestricted mode speculation remains allowed and queries report enabled; in controllable modes per-task disable and sticky force-disable are honored with a barrier when the current task changes; in strict modes queries report disabled. Force-disable blocks later enabling.

L1D flush task choice is a single thread flag that is meaningful only while a conditional-flush feature is active. When inactive, updates fail and queries report forced disable; when active, enable and disable toggle the flag and queries report the current choice with a user-controllable marker.

Thread speculation flags are reconciled lazily from persistent task attributes only when a force-update request is pending, after which the request is consumed; the helper returns the resulting thread flags and the current-task wrapper holds preemption across the refresh.
Entering constrained execution applies the strongest task disable for store bypass and for indirect branches whenever the corresponding global policy selects seccomp-driven management.

Secondary CPU startup reapplies cached speculation control to hardware when the control interface exists and applies a vendor-specific store bypass shutdown under a full-disable global policy. A separate global flag records whether hypervisor handling for an instruction-TLB multi-hit condition is desired.

L1TF mitigation defaults from build configuration, accepts boot-time selection among disabled, flush-oriented, and full variants with optional SMT and warning modifiers, resolves automatic choice using vulnerability presence plus global vulnerability and SMT policies, and applies stronger levels by disabling SMT while enabling an invalid-entry hardware capability when effective.
Cache address width is conservatively raised to a fixed minimum for a bounded set of legacy processors within one CPU family, leaving other families untouched.

Return-stack-overflow mitigation supports disabled, microcode-only, safe-return, and barrier-based options with automatic selection favoring safe-return for kernel or host attack vectors and microcode-only for narrower vectors. Early-generation parts without possible SMT use a dedicated state; missing microcode extension downgrades protection with a notice; build options gate safe-return and barrier paths; a later update may upgrade to barrier mode when another mitigation already uses it, and application programs return thunks or entry and exit barriers while adjusting related capability flags.

Virtual-machine escape mitigation defaults from build configuration, accepts boot-time disable, barrier, or forced-vulnerability choices, resolves automatic mode from vulnerability presence, barrier support, and global policy, upgrades to a VM-exit barrier when sibling mitigations already provide it, and application enables an exit-to-user barrier capability only for the corresponding mode.

Re-evaluation after SMT topology change runs under a single speculation-control mutex, refreshing strict and conditional branch controls, idle-clear and branch-idle states, and emitting one-time warnings when SMT remains active with leak-prone mitigations or without required cross-thread protection.

Early mitigation selection snapshots hardware capabilities, sanitizes any inherited control bits from a previous kernel, announces attack vectors, then chooses every CPU vulnerability mitigation in a fixed order before alternative patching, leaving later phases to refine choices.

Protection can be weakened or voided by excessive physical memory beyond half the addressable range, a low-pagetable build, absent microcode extensions, or leaving SMT enabled with mitigations that assume cross-thread isolation; these cases log warnings and either retain a degraded mode or skip enabling the relevant capability.

User control uses three vulnerability selectors and up to four control requests, with query results encoding user-controllable plus state bits for enable, disable, force-disable, no-exec-after-disable, and unaffected conditions.

Mitigation options are represented as small enumerations with display tables and read-only-after-init current values; VM-escape defines four ordered modes with labels for all but automatic, return-stack-overflow maps each mode to a human-readable status, and virtualization flush policy has a dedicated automatic default.

Externally reachable operations in these fragments comprise current-task speculation refresh, seccomp mitigation hook, speculation-control set and get dispatchers, secondary-CPU setup, SMT re-evaluation, and early mitigation selection.
